people.name: Yazdegerd I
people.fullName: Yazdegerd I, King of Kings of Iran and non-Iran
people.summary: Sasanian king remembered by Christians as tolerant and by Zoroastrian priests as 'the sinner'. He allowed the synod of 410 that organised the Persian church, and Procopius claims Arcadius named him guardian of the infant Theodosius II.
people.death: died in Hyrcania; tradition says kicked to death by a mysterious horse

people.name: Bahram V
people.summary: Son of Yazdegerd I, raised at the Lakhmid court of al-Hira, who won the throne with Arab help in 420. His persecution of Christians caused the Roman war of 421-422; he ended the Arsacid kingdom of Armenia in 428. Persian legend made him the great hunter 'Bahram Gur'.
people.death: disappeared hunting, legend says swallowed by a swamp

people.name: Yazdegerd II
people.summary: Sasanian king who briefly attacked Rome in 440 and spent most of his reign fighting the Kidarites in the east. His attempt to impose Zoroastrianism on Armenia provoked the revolt crushed at Avarayr in 451.

sources.w: History of Vardan and the Armenian War

people.name: Peroz I
people.summary: Sasanian king who seized the throne from his brother Hormizd III with Hephthalite help, then fought the Hephthalites three times, was captured and ransomed, and was killed with his army in 484. His defeats left Persia tributary to the Hephthalites.
people.death: killed in a trench ambush by the Hephthalites, 484

people.name: Mazdak
people.summary: Zoroastrian heterodox preacher whose movement, as reported by hostile sources, demanded the sharing of property and women. Kavad I supported him early in his reign, for which he was deposed in 496; Mazdak and his followers were massacred around 528 at the instigation of Prince Khosrow.

people.name: Hormizd IV
people.summary: Son of Khosrow I and a Turkic princess. He refused Roman peace terms, fought Rome, the Turks and the Khazars simultaneously, executed many nobles and clashed with the priesthood. He humiliated his victorious general Bahram Chobin, provoking the revolt that led to his blinding and death.
people.death: blinded and killed in a palace coup by his brothers-in-law Vistahm and Vinduyih, 590

people.name: Tamkhosrow
people.summary: Persian general who fought the Romans in Armenia and Mesopotamia in 576-582, defeating Justinian son of Germanus in 577. He was killed in the battle of Constantina against Maurice in June 582.
people.death: killed at the battle of Constantina, 582

people.name: Adarmahan
people.summary: Persian general and raider who sacked Apamea and burned the suburbs of Antioch in 573, raided Osrhoene in 581 and was defeated with Tamkhosrow at Constantina in 582.

people.name: Kavad II
people.summary: Son of Khosrow II and his Christian wife Maria (according to tradition), who overthrew and killed his father in February 628, executed his brothers and made peace with Heraclius, returning all Roman territory. He died of plague after about seven months.

people.name: Ardashir III
people.summary: Seven-year-old son of Kavad II, enthroned in 628 under the regent Mah-Adhur Gushnasp. He was killed in April 630 when Shahrbaraz seized Ctesiphon with Roman support.

people.name: Boran
people.summary: Khosrow II's daughter and the first woman to rule the Sasanian empire, from June 630 to 631. She sought to restore order, remit taxes and confirm peace with Heraclius through an embassy of the catholicos Ishoyahb II, and struck coins bearing her portrait.

people.name: Azarmidokht
people.summary: Sister of Boran who ruled briefly in 630-631. She had the spahbed Farrukh Hormizd killed when he sought to marry her and was herself killed by his son Rustam Farrokhzad.
people.death: blinded and killed by Rustam Farrokhzad, 631

people.name: Yazdegerd III
people.summary: Last Sasanian King of Kings, crowned as a child at Istakhr in 632. He lost Mesopotamia at Qadisiyya and Jalula (636-637), the Iranian plateau at Nahavand (642), and fled east through Iran; he was killed near Merv in 651. His son Peroz took refuge at the Tang court.

people.name: Rustam Farrokhzad
people.summary: Persian noble from the Ispahbudhan house of Khurasan who avenged his father's murder by killing Azarmidokht, became the power behind Yazdegerd III and commanded the Persian army at Qadisiyya, where he was killed. Firdawsi's Shahnameh gives him a prophetic lament for Iran.

people.name: Abraha
people.summary: Aksumite general who seized power in Himyar (Yemen) after the Aksumite conquest of 525, defied the Negus and ruled as king, repairing the Marib dam (548) and receiving embassies from Rome and Persia. His inscription records a campaign into central Arabia in 552; Islamic tradition makes him the leader of the elephant expedition against Mecca.

people.name: al-Mundhir III
people.summary: Lakhmid king of al-Hira and Persia's chief Arab ally for half a century. He raided Roman Syria repeatedly, reaching Antioch's territory in 529, fought at Callinicum (531), sacrificed a son of al-Harith to al-Uzza according to Procopius, and was killed by the Ghassanids at the battle of Halima in 554.
people.death: killed in battle against al-Harith ibn Jabala, 554

people.name: al-Harith ibn Jabala

roles.t: Supreme phylarch and king of the Arab federates

people.summary: Ghassanid (Jafnid) ruler made 'king' of Rome's Arab federates by Justinian around 529. He fought at Callinicum (531), killed al-Mundhir III in 554, visited Constantinople in 563, and as a Miaphysite obtained the consecration of Jacob Baradaeus and Theodore as bishops in 542.
scholarship: Shahid, Byzantium and the Arabs in the Sixth Century (1995-2010)

people.name: al-Mundhir ibn al-Harith
people.summary: Son of al-Harith, victorious over the Lakhmids in 570 and 578, who sacked al-Hira. A committed Miaphysite and patron of churches, he quarrelled with Justin II, joined Maurice's failed Euphrates expedition of 581 and was arrested in 582 and exiled to Sicily.

people.name: al-Nu'man III
people.summary: Last Lakhmid king of al-Hira, a Christian convert and patron of poets. Khosrow II, offended by his refusal of a marriage alliance and suspecting disloyalty, deposed and killed him around 602, ending the Lakhmid buffer state.
people.death: killed in Persian custody, c. 602 (tradition: trampled by elephants)

people.name: al-Muthanna ibn Haritha
people.summary: Chief of the Shayban of the Bakr ibn Wa'il whose raids on the Persian frontier drew Medina into Iraq. He served under Khalid, saved the remnant of the army at the Battle of the Bridge (634) and won at al-Buwayb, dying of his wounds before Qadisiyya.

people.name: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas
people.fullName: Sa'd ibn Malik ibn Abi Waqqas
people.summary: Early Companion of Muhammad from the Quraysh who commanded the Arab army at Qadisiyya (636), took Ctesiphon (637) and founded Kufa (638). One of the six electors of Umar's successor, he withdrew from politics during the first civil war and died at his estate near Medina.
people.death: died at al-Aqiq near Medina, c. 674

people.name: Shurahbil ibn Hasana
people.summary: One of the four commanders sent by Abu Bakr to Syria in 633-634; he took Bostra, fought at Ajnadayn, Fahl and the Yarmuk, and conquered much of Jordan and Galilee. He died in the plague of Amwas.

people.name: Marcian
people.summary: Patrician and cousin of Justin II who opened the Persian war of 572 by raiding Arzanene and besieged Nisibis in 573, until Justin humiliatingly dismissed him in front of his troops, provoking the panic that preceded the loss of Dara.

people.name: Justinian son of Germanus
people.summary: Son of Justinian I's cousin Germanus and brother of the murdered Justin. He fought in Italy and commanded in the East, sharing in the victory at Melitene (576) before his defeat in Armenia (577). He was suspected of plotting against Tiberius II, who forgave him.

people.name: Peter
people.summary: Maurice's brother, made curopalates, who replaced Priscus in Thrace (594) and commanded again in 601-602. Theophylact, following sources favourable to Priscus, portrays him as incompetent. He was killed by Phocas's men after Maurice's fall.
people.death: killed after the fall of Maurice, 602

people.name: Constantina
people.fullName: Constantina Augusta, daughter of Tiberius II
people.summary: Daughter of Tiberius II and Ino-Anastasia, married to Maurice in 582, mother of nine children including Theodosius. After Maurice's murder she was confined with her daughters, implicated in a plot and executed with them at Chalcedon.
people.death: executed with her three daughters at the harbour of Eutropius, c. 605-607

people.name: Theodosius
people.summary: Maurice's eldest son, crowned co-emperor in 590 and married to the daughter of the patrician Germanus. Sent to seek Persian help in 602, he was overtaken and killed; rumours of his survival let Khosrow II sponsor a pretender in his name.
people.death: killed near Nicaea on Phocas's orders, 602

people.name: Narses
people.summary: Persarmenian-born Roman general, distinct from Justinian's eunuch, who led the army that restored Khosrow II at the Blarathon (591). He rebelled against Phocas at Edessa (603) and, surrendering on a safe-conduct, was burned alive.

people.name: Heraclius the Elder
people.summary: Armenian-born general who distinguished himself at Solachon (586) and Sisarbanon (589), then as exarch of Africa raised the revolt against Phocas in 608 with his brother Gregory, sending his son Heraclius by sea and nephew Nicetas by land. He died soon after his son's coronation.

people.name: Nicetas
people.summary: Cousin of Heraclius who won Egypt from Phocas's forces in 608-610, governed it as patrician and fought beside Heraclius at Antioch (613). He held Alexandria until the Persian conquest of 619. His daughter married Heraclius's son Constantine III.

people.name: Bonosus
people.summary: Phocas's ruthless comes Orientis who crushed the riots of Antioch (609) and was sent to Egypt against Nicetas, by whom he was defeated. He was killed when Heraclius took Constantinople.

people.name: Fabia-Eudokia
people.summary: African noblewoman betrothed to Heraclius, held hostage by Phocas, and crowned and married to him on 5 October 610. She bore Epiphania and Constantine III and died of epilepsy in August 612.

people.name: Romanus
people.summary: Exarch of Ravenna who coordinated with the Frankish invasion of 590, recovered towns in the Po valley and the Via Amerina corridor (592), and opposed Gregory the Great's separate negotiations with the Lombards.

people.name: Gennadius
people.fullName: Gennadius, magister militum and exarch of Africa
people.summary: Roman commander in Africa who killed the Moorish king Garmul (578) and is the first attested exarch of Africa (591), corresponding with Gregory the Great about the Donatists and church estates.

people.name: Eleutherius
people.summary: Eunuch exarch of Ravenna who suppressed the killers of his predecessor and the rebel John of Conza, then proclaimed himself emperor in 619 and was killed by his soldiers on the way to Rome.
people.death: killed by his troops at Castrum Luceoli, 619

people.name: Hypatius
people.summary: Nephew of Anastasius I, an unlucky general captured by Vitalian (513) and beaten by the Persians at Amida (503). In the Nika riot the crowd crowned him emperor in the Hippodrome against his will; he was executed the next day.
people.death: executed after the Nika riot, January 532

people.name: John nephew of Vitalian
people.summary: Bold and insubordinate commander in the Gothic war, nicknamed 'the Sanguinary', who seized Ariminum (538), sided with Narses against Belisarius, married Germanus's daughter Justina and fought at Taginae (552).

people.name: Stotzas
people.summary: Bodyguard soldier who led the great mutiny of the African army in 536, besieged Carthage, was beaten by Belisarius and Germanus (Scalae Veteres, 537) and fought on with the Moors until killed in single combat with John at Thacia in 545.

people.name: Chrysaphius
people.summary: Eunuch who dominated Theodosius II's court in the 440s, ousted Pulcheria's and Eudocia's influence, supported Eutyches and Ephesus II, and plotted the assassination of Attila in 449. Marcian executed him in 450.

people.name: Eutychius
people.summary: Patriarch who presided over the council of 553, was deposed by Justinian in 565 for rejecting aphthartodocetism, and returned in 577, when he debated with Gregory (the future pope) on the nature of the resurrected body.

people.name: John of Ephesus
people.fullName: John of Amida, Miaphysite bishop of Ephesus
people.summary: Syriac Miaphysite historian from Amida, who under Justinian led missions that he claimed converted 80,000 pagans in Asia Minor, then was imprisoned under Justin II. His Lives of the Eastern Saints and Ecclesiastical History, Part III of which survives complete, are key sources for the plague, Justin II's madness and the Slavs.

people.name: Timothy Aelurus
people.summary: Anti-Chalcedonian patriarch of Alexandria consecrated in 457, implicated in the murder of Proterius, exiled to Gangra and Cherson (460-475), and restored by Basiliscus. His nickname means 'the Cat' or 'the Weasel'.

people.name: Simeon the Stylite

roles.t: Ascetic on a column near Telanissos

people.summary: Syrian shepherd turned ascetic who lived on a column for some 36 years, preaching to crowds and advising emperors; Theodoret, who knew him, wrote his life. His cult produced the pilgrimage complex of Qal'at Sim'an.

people.name: John Cassian
people.summary: Monk from Scythia Minor who lived in Bethlehem and among the Egyptian desert fathers, was ordained deacon by John Chrysostom, and founded monasteries at Marseille. His Institutes and Conferences shaped western monasticism.

people.name: Patrick
people.summary: Romano-British son of a decurion, kidnapped by Irish raiders at sixteen, who escaped and later returned to Ireland as a bishop. His Confessio and Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus are unique first-person sources for fifth-century Britain and Ireland.

people.name: Honoratus
people.summary: Gallo-Roman aristocrat who founded the island monastery of Lérins around 410 and became bishop of Arles; his kinsman Hilary wrote his Life.

people.name: Caesarius of Arles
people.summary: Monk of Lérins and bishop of Arles under Visigothic, Ostrogothic and Frankish rulers. He presided at the councils of Agde (506) and Orange (529), which settled the grace controversy, wrote some 250 popular sermons and the first Rule for nuns.

people.name: Benedict of Nursia
people.summary: Umbrian who abandoned studies in Rome for a hermit's cave at Subiaco, founded monasteries there and around 529 at Monte Cassino, where he wrote his Rule. Almost everything known of him comes from Book 2 of Gregory the Great's Dialogues, including his meeting with Totila in 542.
people.death: died at Monte Cassino, traditionally 21 March 547

people.name: Dionysius Exiguus
people.summary: Scythian monk ('the Small', from his humility) in Rome who translated Greek canons and decretals into Latin, creating the Collectio Dionysiana, and in 525 devised the Easter tables counting years from the Incarnation.

people.name: Romanos the Melode
people.summary: Syrian-born deacon from Emesa who served in Constantinople under Anastasius and Justinian and composed the greatest Byzantine kontakia; legend says the Theotokos gave him the gift of song in a dream.

people.name: Cosmas Indicopleustes
people.summary: Alexandrian merchant who travelled to Aksum and the Red Sea, later a monk, author of the Christian Topography (c. 550) with its Tabernacle-shaped cosmos and valuable notes on Indian Ocean trade.

people.name: Priscian
people.summary: Grammarian from Caesarea in Mauretania who taught Latin in Constantinople and wrote the Institutiones Grammaticae, the most comprehensive Latin grammar from antiquity and the standard textbook of the Middle Ages.

people.name: Corippus
people.summary: African Latin poet, author of the Iohannis on John Troglita's Moorish wars and of the panegyric In laudem Iustini minoris (566), which describes Justinian's funeral and Justin II's coronation ceremonies in detail.

people.name: Gildas
people.summary: British monk and author of De Excidio Britanniae, the only substantial narrative of the end of Roman Britain by an insular writer; later Breton tradition linked him to Rhuys.

people.name: Venantius Fortunatus
people.summary: Italian poet from near Treviso, educated at Ravenna, who crossed into Gaul in 566, wrote an epithalamium for Sigibert and Brunhild, and settled at Poitiers as friend of Radegund. His hymns Vexilla regis and Pange lingua were written for the True Cross relic of 569.

people.name: Radegund
people.summary: Thuringian princess captured as a child by Chlothar I and married to him; after he killed her brother she left him and founded the convent of the Holy Cross at Poitiers, obtaining a relic of the True Cross from Justin II.

people.name: Isidore of Seville
people.summary: Younger brother of Leander, bishop of Seville for 36 years and the most influential scholar of Visigothic Spain. He wrote the Etymologies, the History of the Goths, On the Nature of Things, Chronicles and On Famous Men, and presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo (633).

people.name: Leander of Seville
people.summary: Hispano-Roman bishop from a Cartagena family who converted Hermenegild, met Gregory the Great in Constantinople (where Gregory dedicated the Moralia to him), and guided Reccared's conversion and the Third Council of Toledo.

people.name: Columbanus
people.summary: Irish monk who founded Annegray, Luxeuil and Fontaine in Burgundy, defied Brunhild and Theuderic II and was expelled in 610, then founded Bobbio in Lombard Italy. His letters to popes defend Irish Easter reckoning in remarkably blunt Latin.

people.name: Maximus the Confessor
people.summary: Former imperial secretary under Heraclius who became a monk and the leading theologian of dyotheletism, opposing the Ekthesis from Africa. He was condemned under Constans II, had his tongue and right hand cut off, and died in exile in Lazica.
people.death: died in exile in Lazica, 13 August 662

people.name: Honorius I
people.summary: Campanian pope who restored Roman churches, including Sant'Agnese fuori le mura and the bronze roof tiles of St Peter's from the temple of Venus and Rome, and supported the English mission. His letter accepting 'one will' in Christ led to his posthumous anathema in 681.

people.name: Benjamin I
people.fullName: Benjamin I, Coptic patriarch of Alexandria
people.summary: Miaphysite patriarch of Alexandria who fled to Upper Egypt when Cyrus arrived in 631 and spent ten years in hiding. After the Arab conquest Amr ibn al-As restored him to Alexandria; he rebuilt the Coptic church under Muslim rule.

sources.a: History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria

people.name: Leovigild
people.summary: The most successful Visigothic king. He took Asidona and Córdoba (571-572), subdued Cantabria and Orospeda, founded Reccopolis (578), crushed his son Hermenegild's revolt (579-584) and annexed the Suebic kingdom (585). He adopted throne, crown and imperial-style coinage and tried to reconcile Catholics with a modified Arianism.

people.name: Hermenegild
people.summary: Elder son of Leovigild, married to the Frankish princess Ingund, who converted to Catholicism and rebelled at Seville in 579, striking coins with the legend 'Regi a Deo vita'. Captured in 584, he was killed at Tarragona in 585 and honoured by Gregory the Great as a martyr.

people.name: Reccared I
people.summary: Younger son of Leovigild who converted to Catholicism in 587 and led the Goths into the Catholic church at the Third Council of Toledo (589), suppressing Arian plots. His general Claudius defeated the Franks at Carcassonne (589). He took the imperial name Flavius.

people.name: Sisebut
people.summary: Learned Visigothic king who wrote a Life of Desiderius of Vienne and an astronomical poem, campaigned against Roman Spania and the Asturians, built a fleet, and ordered the forced baptism of the Jews. Isidore dedicated On the Nature of Things to him.

people.name: Suintila
people.summary: Visigothic king who completed the conquest of Roman Spania around 624-625, earning Isidore's praise as the first king of all Spain; he was deposed by Sisenand with Frankish help in 631 and condemned by the Fourth Council of Toledo.

people.name: Theudis
people.summary: Ostrogothic officer who governed Visigothic Spain for Theodoric, married a rich Hispano-Roman heiress, and became king after Amalaric's murder in 531. He failed to take Septem (Ceuta) from the Romans in 547 and was assassinated in his palace.

people.name: Theudebert I
people.summary: Grandson of Clovis, king at Reims, who extended Frankish power over Alamannia, Provence and parts of northern Italy, invaded Italy in 539, and was the first barbarian king to strike gold solidi in his own name. A letter to Justinian boasts of his dominion from the Danube to the Ocean.

people.name: Sigibert I
people.summary: Son of Chlothar I and king at Reims and Metz from 561, husband of the Visigothic princess Brunhild, who fought the Avars in 562 and 566 and his brother Chilperic for most of his reign, until he was assassinated at Vitry in 575.
people.death: stabbed by Fredegund's agents at Vitry, 575

people.name: Chilperic I
people.summary: Son of Chlothar I, king at Soissons, who murdered his Visigothic wife Galswintha to marry Fredegund, waged war on Sigibert, wrote Latin hymns and a treatise on the Trinity, and proposed new letters for the alphabet. Gregory of Tours called him the Nero and Herod of the age.

people.name: Guntram
people.summary: Son of Chlothar I, king of Burgundy at Chalon, mediator between his warring brothers and protector of his nephews. He crushed the pretender Gundovald (585), concluded the Treaty of Andelot (587) and was venerated as a saint for his piety.

people.name: Brunhild

roles.t: Regent for her son and grandsons

people.summary: Visigothic princess, daughter of Athanagild, married to Sigibert I in 567. After his murder she governed Austrasia and Burgundy for her son Childebert II and grandsons, corresponded with Gregory the Great and Maurice, and fought a long feud with Fredegund. Chlothar II had her torn apart by horses in 613.

people.name: Fredegund
people.summary: Servant who became Chilperic I's wife after the murder of Galswintha; Gregory of Tours accuses her of the assassinations of Sigibert I and Bishop Praetextatus among others. She preserved the throne of her infant son Chlothar II.

people.name: Chlothar II
people.summary: Son of Chilperic and Fredegund, king from infancy, who destroyed Brunhild and her great-grandsons in 613 and reunited Francia, issuing the Edict of Paris (614) and making his son Dagobert king of Austrasia (623).

people.name: Dagobert I
people.summary: Last powerful Merovingian, who ruled from Paris, made treaties with Heraclius, intervened in Visigothic Spain (631), fought Samo's Wends (631) and endowed the abbey of Saint-Denis, where he was buried.

people.name: Gundovald
people.summary: Claimant to be a son of Chlothar I, mocked as 'Ballomer', who lived in Constantinople and returned with imperial money in 582. Raised on a shield at Brive in 584, he was besieged at Convenae and killed in 585.

people.name: Mummolus
people.summary: Gallo-Roman general of Guntram who defeated Lombard and Saxon invaders (570s) and later defected to Gundovald; he was killed after betraying the pretender at Convenae in 585.

people.name: Authari
people.summary: Son of Cleph elected king in 584 to restore Lombard unity against Franks and Romans. He married the Bavarian Catholic princess Theodelinda in 589 and reportedly rode to Reggio and touched a column in the sea, claiming Italy to that point.

people.name: Agilulf
people.summary: Thuringian-born duke of Turin chosen by Theodelinda as husband and king in 590. He threatened Rome (593), made truces brokered by Gregory the Great, took Padua, Cremona and Mantua (601-603), granted Bobbio to Columbanus and allowed his son's Catholic baptism. A gilded plaque from his helmet shows him enthroned.

people.name: Theodelinda
people.summary: Bavarian Catholic princess, wife of Authari and then Agilulf, friend and correspondent of Gregory the Great, who built the basilica of St John at Monza and promoted the conversion of the Lombards. The Monza treasury preserves gifts associated with her.

people.name: Rothari
people.summary: Arian duke of Brescia, king from 636, who conquered Liguria and Oderzo from the Romans and in 643 issued the Edict of Rothari, the first written code of Lombard law, in 388 chapters.

people.name: Zotto
people.summary: First Lombard duke of Benevento, who carved out an autonomous duchy in southern Italy and whose men destroyed Monte Cassino.

people.name: Istämi
people.summary: Ruler of the western wing of the Turkic khaganate, called Sizabul or Silziboulos by Menander, who destroyed the Hephthalites with Khosrow I and then allied with Justin II against Persia, receiving the embassy of Zemarchus (569).

people.name: Kubrat
people.summary: Bulgar ruler raised at Constantinople who threw off Avar rule around 635 and allied with Heraclius, who made him a patrician. His sons, according to Byzantine tradition, divided his people, one of them, Asparukh, founding the Danubian Bulgar state in 681.

people.name: Samo
people.summary: Frankish merchant who, according to Fredegar, led the Wends in revolt against the Avars and ruled them as king for 35 years, defeating Dagobert I at Wogastisburg (631).

people.name: Dengizich
people.summary: Son of Attila who tried to restore Hunnic power after the Nedao, demanding trade rights from Leo I, and invaded the empire across the Danube; he was killed by the general Anagast in 469.
people.death: killed in battle; head displayed in Constantinople, 469

people.name: Theodahad
people.summary: Nephew of Theodoric and wealthy Tuscan landowner with Platonic interests, made co-ruler by Amalasuntha in 534. He had her murdered, gave Justinian his casus belli, negotiated secretly to abdicate, and was deposed and killed after the fall of Naples.
people.death: killed while fleeing to Ravenna, December 536

people.name: Hilderic
people.summary: Son of Huneric and the Theodosian princess Eudocia, pro-Roman king of the Vandals who ended persecution of Catholics. Deposed by Gelimer in 530, he was killed in 533 as Belisarius approached Carthage.

people.name: Mermeroes
people.summary: Veteran Persian general of the Lazic war, who besieged Archaeopolis (551) and, though crippled by age and carried in a litter, kept the Persians in Lazica until his death.

people.name: Mesrop Mashtots
people.summary: Armenian former royal secretary and monk who invented the Armenian alphabet around 405 and, according to his pupil Koriwn, the Georgian and Albanian scripts, organising the translation of the Bible and Greek and Syriac texts.

people.name: Gerontius
people.summary: British-born general of Constantine III who cleared the Pyrenean passes, then rebelled in 409 with his own emperor Maximus. Deserted by his troops in 411, he died in a last stand with his Alan follower and his wife.
people.death: killed himself and his wife in his burning house in Spain, 411

people.name: Sabas
people.summary: Cappadocian monk who founded the Great Lavra (483) and other monasteries in the Judaean desert, led the Chalcedonian monks of Palestine against Anastasius, and petitioned Justinian for tax relief after the Samaritan revolt of 529.
people.death: died at the Great Lavra, 5 December 532

people.name: Musaylima
people.fullName: Maslama ibn Habib of the Banu Hanifa
people.summary: Prophet of the Banu Hanifa of Yamama, called by Muslim tradition the 'little Maslama' (Musaylima) and 'the Liar', who claimed revelation in Muhammad's lifetime and led the strongest resistance of the Ridda. He was killed at Aqraba by the spear of Wahshi, the slave who had killed Hamza at Uhud.
people.death: killed at the battle of Yamama, c. December 632

people.name: John of Biclaro
people.summary: Goth from Scallabis educated for seventeen years in Constantinople, exiled to Barcelona by Leovigild for his Catholicism, founder of the monastery of Biclaro and bishop of Gerona. His chronicle of 567-590 is the main source for Leovigild and Reccared.

people.name: Shirin
people.summary: Christian, probably Aramaean, wife of Khosrow II, patron of the Miaphysite church at court, whose pregnancy prompted Khosrow's votive gifts to St Sergius. Persian romance made her the heroine of Nizami's Khosrow and Shirin.

people.name: Theodoric II
people.summary: Visigothic king who murdered his brother Thorismund, made Avitus emperor (455), crushed the Suebi at the Órbigo (456) and expanded into Spain and Narbonensis. Sidonius Apollinaris left a celebrated portrait of his daily routine at Toulouse. His brother Euric murdered him in 466.

people.name: Iyad ibn Ghanm
people.summary: Arab commander who succeeded Abu Ubayda in northern Syria and conquered Roman Mesopotamia (Edessa, Harran, Amida, Dara and Callinicum) in 639-640, mostly by capitulation.
